name: Double-jaw surgery for retrognathia

card.summary: Bimaxillary (upper and lower jaw) surgery that moves a recessed mandible forward, often with the maxilla and chin; a major established operation with documented joint and nerve risks.
card.aka: Bimaxillary surgery, bimax, BSSO plus Le Fort I, DJS
card.note: Major surgery: reported complications include nerve injury, infection and condylar changes; forum users debate single-jaw versus double-jaw plans.

quick.overview:
Double-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery repositions both the upper and lower jaw, usually after orthodontic preparation, to correct a recessed lower jaw (retrognathia), bite problems and facial proportions. It is a long-established operation in oral and maxillofacial surgery, and sometimes is combined with a genioplasty.

In looksmaxxing communities it sits at the top of the 'hardmaxxing' ladder, and members discuss whether a single-jaw plan can do the job.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons cut the jaws (typically a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the mandible and a Le Fort I osteotomy of the maxilla), move them to a planned position, and fix them with plates and screws. Planning uses imaging and often 3D software.
quick.risks: Reported risks include temporary or permanent numbness from nerve injury, infection, bleeding and swelling, and in some patients condylar atrophy or joint changes after bimaxillary surgery. Recovery is typically measured in weeks to months.

lead: Double-jaw surgery, or bimaxillary surgery, is an orthognathic operation in which both the maxilla (upper jaw) and the mandible (lower jaw) are cut, repositioned and fixed. For retrognathia, a recessed lower jaw, the mandible is advanced, commonly through a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, and the upper jaw is moved to match the bite. [1][2] The aim is a lower face that projects further, a better-defined jawline and chin, and a bite that closes properly, so that the profile looks more balanced from the side as well as the front.

Orthognathic surgery is described as corrective jaw surgery usually done through the mouth, in coordination with an orthodontist. Encyclopedic accounts trace its development from a case published in 1849 through the mid-twentieth-century popularisation of the sagittal split by Hugo Obwegeser. [1] A 1957 paper on correction of mandibular prognathism and retrognathia considered genioplasty as part of surgical reshaping of the chin. [3]

Published reviews report that the operations achieve large and generally stable skeletal changes: a 2026 systematic review of 65 studies and 6,482 patients found a mean ANB-angle improvement of 5.4 degrees for Class II correction, skeletal stability at one year or more in 87.3 percent, and patient satisfaction of 87.6 percent, higher for aesthetic than functional outcomes, alongside a 32.4 percent overall complication rate that was mostly minor. [10]

In looksmaxxing forums, double-jaw surgery is discussed as a major hardmaxxing option at the top of the surgical ladder, with threads comparing it with single-jaw surgery plus genioplasty, and with members describing diagnoses of retrognathia. [4][5][1]

chain: Upper and lower jaws are cut and moved to planned positions
Fixation with plates and screws holds the new position
Recessed lower face projects forward with a corrected bite
angle.text: For a recessed lower jaw, surgery moves the skeleton itself, so chin and jaw projection change from the profile view and the bite is corrected at the same time. People pursue it for profile balance, jaw definition and functional reasons such as bite and airway.

paras: Orthognathic surgery addresses jaw structure and growth problems, airway issues including sleep apnea, joint disorders, malocclusion and facial asymmetry or proportion. [1] The bilateral sagittal split osteotomy moves the mandible forward or backward, and Le Fort I-type osteotomy repositions the upper jaw. [1] Genioplasty moves the chin forward or back through intraoral cuts with plate fixation and may be added to the jaw operations. [1][13]

Retrognathia is described as an abnormal backward positioning of the maxilla or mandible, particularly the mandible, relative to the facial skeleton, and it is sometimes called an overbite in lay usage although the term is not used medically. [15] It may occur on its own or in syndromes such as Treacher Collins syndrome. [15] Wikipedia's orthognathic article estimates that close to 5 percent of people in the UK or US have dentofacial deformities that could warrant surgery. [1]

Chin augmentation by implants or fillers is described as an alternative way to change the profile, but the article notes orthognathic surgery is used when a small chin coexists with a significant overbite, since cosmetic chin procedures do not change the bite. [13]

Wikipedia credits Simon P. Hullihen with publishing one of the first known jaw-surgery cases in 1849, notes that Harold Hargis coined the term orthognathic, and that the sagittal split osteotomy was developed and popularised by Hugo Obwegeser. [1] Jaw osteotomies were done from the 1940s. [1] A 1957 surgical paper described correction of mandibular prognathism and retrognathia and reshaping of the chin. [3]

By the 2000s approaches changed: Wikipedia reports that Raffaini introduced orthognathic surgery under local anaesthesia with intravenous sedation in 2002, where patients had previously been fully sedated and hospitalised for two to three days, and notes a shift in the field from mainly dental goals toward sleep-apnea and aesthetic uses. [1] Maxillomandibular advancement (moving both jaws forward) was applied to obstructive sleep apnea after the late 1970s, when advancing the lower jaw was noted to improve sleepiness in three patients. [14]

A multidisciplinary team of oral and maxillofacial surgeons and orthodontists, sometimes with speech therapists, plans the surgery using radiographs, photographs and 3D prediction software, and a psychological assessment is occasionally needed. [1] Presurgical orthodontics traditionally takes up to a year, with newer approaches including surgery-first and clear aligners. [1]

In the operation, the jaws are cut, moved to the planned position and stabilised with titanium plates and screws. [1] A 2026 meta-analysis found patient-specific guides and implants showed smaller linear deviations than CAD/CAM occlusal splints on three axes across 30 studies, with no significant difference in complications. [17]

Wikipedia reports initial healing of 2 to 6 weeks, with full bone union and remodelling over a further 2 to 4 months; jaw immobilisation, when used, lasts about 1 to 4 weeks; patients usually follow a liquid diet, often lose weight, and have swelling that can last months. [1] Return to work is described as possible in 2 to 6 weeks, with recovery rules applying for about 8 weeks. [1]

The 2026 Frontiers in Oral Health systematic review of 65 studies and 6,482 patients reported mean ANB improvements of 6.8 degrees for Class III and 5.4 degrees for Class II correction, skeletal stability of 87.3 percent at one year or more, relapse greater than 2 mm in 18.7 percent, and a pooled improvement on the OQLQ quality-of-life questionnaire (standardised mean difference -1.84). Satisfaction was 87.6 percent and was higher for aesthetic than functional outcomes. [10]

A 2026 prospective study of 101 women compared orthodontic treatment with combined orthodontic-surgical treatment: both groups improved in overall quality of life at three months, with surgery improving emotional, social and total scores but not oral-symptom or functional-limitation scores. [18] A 2026 cross-sectional study of 81 adults with Class III malocclusion found that women reported less social self-confidence than men before surgery, though no difference survived across all comparisons. [18]

Encyclopedic accounts list bleeding, swelling, infection, and nerve damage causing facial numbness, which is usually temporary but rarely permanent; infection rates of up to 7% are reported. [2][1] Numbness from injury to the inferior alveolar nerve typically recovers within three months. [1] Wikipedia also reports that maxillary impaction carries more risk than some other movements, and that removal of third molars during osteotomy was linked to hardware infection in a 1987-1991 series of 83 patients. [1]

A 2015 systematic review of complications covered 44 studies selected from 1,924 articles and concluded that the complications associated with orthognathic surgery are numerous and varied. [11] A 2015 review of inferior alveolar nerve injury after sagittal split osteotomy drew on 61 reports and attributed wide variation in reported incidence to a lack of standardised assessment, noting that 26 percent of reports did not give incidence. [11] The 2026 review above reported neurosensory disturbance in 52.8 percent of patients with 92.6 percent recovering by 12 months and 3.4 percent permanent. [10]

A 1984 review examined complications after mandibular sagittal split osteotomy, and a 1990 paper reported condylar atrophy and osteoarthrosis after bimaxillary surgery. [6][7] A 2026 meta-analysis comparing maxillomandibular advancement for sleep apnea with orthognathic surgeries for dentofacial deformity reported neurosensory disturbance of 44.9 percent after bimaxillary surgery. [12]

Maxillomandibular advancement, moving both jaws forward, is described as one of the most effective surgical treatments for obstructive sleep apnea, often used after other treatments have been tried; recovery is longer than other sleep surgeries because bone must heal in the new position. [14] A 2026 meta-analysis of 14 studies with at least two years' follow-up found the skeletal advancement held (SNA about 6 degrees, SNB about 5 degrees) and apnea-hypopnea index fell by 40 events per hour, with low certainty and substantial heterogeneity. [12] Another 2026 comparison reported a 79.6 percent surgical success rate and 39 percent cure rate for MMA, with higher infection and hardware-removal rates than bimaxillary surgery for dentofacial deformity. [12]

A looksmax.org thread discusses single-jaw surgery combined with genioplasty for skeletal class II retrognathia compared with double-jaw surgery, referring to a study comparing conventional bimaxillary surgery with single-jaw surgery using autorotation. [4] A reply states that both jaws usually need to be moved because of the bite plane and tooth alignment unless one jaw is already well positioned. [4]
Another thread describes an individual seeing a maxillofacial surgeon about retrognathia and hoping the diagnosis supports reconstructive treatment. [5]

Published literature includes the 1957 surgical description [3], a 1984 complications review of sagittal split osteotomy [6], a 1990 study of condylar atrophy and osteoarthrosis after bimaxillary surgery [7], 2015 systematic reviews of complications and nerve injury [11], and 2026 systematic reviews of skeletal outcomes, quality of life and sleep-apnea advancement. [10][12] Registered trials of retrognathia are mostly of non-surgical orthodontic treatments, such as functional appliances and clear-aligner mandibular advancement. [8][9]

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known jaw-surgery cases. [1]
Paper on correction of mandibular prognathism and retrognathia with genioplasty is published. [3]
Advancing the lower jaw is noted to relieve sleepiness in sleep-apnea patients, leading to maxillomandibular advancement. [14]
Complications after mandibular sagittal split osteotomy are reviewed. [6]
Condylar atrophy and osteoarthrosis after bimaxillary surgery reported. [7]
Raffaini introduces orthognathic surgery under local anaesthesia with sedation. [1]
Systematic reviews of orthognathic complications and inferior alveolar nerve injury are published. [11]
Systematic review of 65 studies on outcomes, complications and quality of life is published. [10]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, double-jaw surgery appears in planning threads and discussions of whether a recessed lower jaw can be treated with one jaw operation plus genioplasty. [4][5]

claims.claim: Single-jaw surgery plus genioplasty can match double-jaw results
claims.believers: A poster planning upper-jaw movement with genioplasty cites a study reporting similar absolute movements between the groups and asks why more single-jaw cases are not seen. [4]
claims.experts: Surgical practice generally plans movements around bite and tooth alignment; a forum reply states that both jaws usually need moving unless one jaw is well positioned. No controlled trial has been reported. [4]

claims.claim: Retrognathia is a diagnosable skeletal deformity that can be treated surgically
claims.believers: One poster describes seeing a maxillofacial surgeon and hoping the diagnosis supports reconstructive treatment. [5]
claims.experts: Orthognathic surgery is an established specialty for jaw position problems, with documented risks including nerve injury and condylar changes. [2][7]

claims.claim: Double-jaw surgery produces a permanent, large change in jaw projection and profile
claims.believers: Forum members planning surgery treat bimaxillary operations as the route to a changed lower face when the jaws are recessed.[4][5]
claims.experts: A 2026 systematic review reported mean ANB improvement of 5.4 degrees for Class II correction with 87.3 percent skeletal stability at one year or more and relapse over 2 mm in 18.7 percent.[10]

claims.claim: Surgery carries lasting numbness or nerve risk that forum members weigh against the benefit
claims.believers: Planning threads discuss single-jaw alternatives partly to limit what must be cut.[4]
claims.experts: Reviews report that neurosensory disturbance is common early, with 92.6 percent recovering by 12 months and 3.4 percent permanent in one 2026 review, and that reporting is inconsistent.[10][11]
